subject: Post-call: TTFT & streaming requirements (SLO qualification)
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>

Cc: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>, Rafael Mendes <rafael_mendes@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-02-10T15:20:00-08:00
Subject: Post-call: TTFT & streaming requirements (SLO qualification)

Thanks again for taking the time today — great discussion. Quick recap and proposed next steps from our side so we have alignment on SLOs and what we should validate in the POC.

Summary of requirements you shared:
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT) targets: Desktop primary flows <= 100ms (p95 target), Mobile / fallback <= 150ms (p95).
- Streaming: prefer Server-Sent Events (SSE) for web UI, WebSocket acceptable for persistent connections. Chunk cadence target: <= 100ms between chunks for a smooth typing experience; ideal cadence 50–80ms.
- Throughput & concurrency: baseline steady-state of ~50 req/s for the feature, with spikes up to 200 concurrent open streams/users during peak.
- Accuracy: want minimal change to model outputs vs your baseline model; we'll include evals in the POC.

Attached: Redwood-SLO-Proposal.pdf (high-level POC plan) and TTFT-measurement-guide.txt (how we measure TTFT for consistency).

Proposed next steps:
1) Technical POC: 2–4 hour load tests using your representative prompt set (you can attach or share a Drive link) to measure TTFT (p50/p95/p99), chunk cadence, and error rates.
2) Config proposal: Rafael will propose a recommended stack (model variant, quantization profile, batching policy, caching) for the latency profile.
3) Commercial: I'll follow up with the POC SOW and a draft PO path; we can discuss Dedicated vs Hosted implications after the POC numbers are in.

Availability: We can run the POC as soon as Feb 18–19. Please confirm the prompt set and whether you prefer SSE or WebSocket for the POC.

Thanks,
Marissa

marissa@redwood.com

Thanks Marissa — appreciate the clear recap. A few clarifying Qs from our engineering side before we lock the POC window:

1) Can you confirm precisely how you measure TTFT? Is it time from our client request leaving the browser, or time from request received by Redwood runtime to first token emitted? We need consistency with our frontend metrics.
2) For streaming: we prefer SSE for our web clients (no stateful connection). Are there differences in achievable TTFT between SSE and WebSocket on your platform?
3) Chunk cadence: you mentioned 50–80ms ideal. How does that interact with small token sizes — does frequency increase network overhead and affect TTFT p95?
4) For Dedicated vs Hosted: we need to understand if Redwood can commit to an SLO (contractual) for TTFT p95 on Dedicated capacity, and what margin you’d expect relative to the target (e.g., 100ms target -> committed 120ms?).

We can share a sample prompt set — here's a link to a short Google Doc with 120 prompts: https://docs.google.com/document/d/retailco-ttft-sample-prompts. Also, our infra team needs the test plan and your required egress IPs for firewall whitelisting.

If you can answer the measurement and SSE/WebSocket differences we can confirm Feb 18.

—Jordan

From: Rafael Mendes <rafael_mendes@redwood.com>
To: Jordan Smith <jordan.smith@retailco.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-02-12T11:47:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Post-call: TTFT & streaming requirements (SLO qualification)

Hi Jordan — good questions. I'll keep this pragmatic and call out what we measure, expected numbers, and tuning levers.

How we measure TTFT
- Our TTFT is measured at the Redwood runtime: time from Redwood's ingress receiving the request (post-LB) to first token emitted into the streaming channel. We provide network delta guidance separately so you can map to client-observed metrics (browser->LB->runtime). For most US regions network delta is ~20–40ms median, varies by carrier.

SSE vs WebSocket
- Protocol difference is minimal for server processing. WebSocket avoids some HTTP reheaders but for a single short-lived stream SSE vs WS typically shows <5–15ms median difference on our infra. Choice should be driven by client architecture.

Chunk cadence and tokenization tradeoffs
- Chunk cadence target (50–80ms) means we flush partial outputs from the runtime that often. Smaller flush intervals improve perceived responsiveness but increase per-chunk overhead (HTTP framing + TLS). For typical prompts we find a sweet spot of 50–80ms with chunk sizes ~1–6 tokens per chunk for conversational workloads.
- At p95 the additional framing overhead is usually within 10–20ms if network latency is low; however, if you are running mobile clients over cellular the framing can add variance. We can adjust flush interval dynamically based on active RTT.

Latency numbers (ballpark, p95) on Dedicated A100-style hosts with low-noise tenancy:
- Medium-size model (7B, quantized): TTFT p95 ~ 30–60ms
- Large model (13B, quantized): TTFT p95 ~ 60–110ms
- Heavy models (70B, q4): TTFT p95 ~ 90–160ms (depends on sequence length and KV cache warmness)

Recommended configuration for your targets (desktop p95 <=100ms):
- Use a 13B or optimized 7B model variant with quantization profile we will propose.
- Keep batching minimal (batch size 1) for low TTFT path, enable continuous KV cache for repeated sessions.
- Enable dynamic flush interval at 50ms for desktop; fall back to 80–100ms on higher RTT endpoints to avoid wasted frames.
- Autoscale reserved capacity to handle 50 req/s steady and headroom for bursts to 200 concurrent open streams; we recommend 2x headroom for warm caches.

Throughput & concurrency
- With the above config, one Dedicated slice (N GPU-equivalent) can sustain ~60–120 concurrent low-latency streams depending on model size and token emission rate. We'll size the POC to replicate your peak and provide an exact capacity plan.

POC plan items we need from you:
- Representative prompt set (thanks for the Doc link)
- Expected average response length and typical prompt length (tokens)
- Egress IPs for firewall rules

Deliverables from POC
- p50/p95/p99 TTFT measured at runtime and mapped to client-observed metrics
- Chunk cadence histogram and per-chunk size distribution
- Error rates and suggestions for configuration changes

We can commit to running the POC Feb 18–19. After POC we can discuss a contractual SLO; for Dedicated offerings we typically accept p95 latency SLOs with agreed warmup windows and traffic profiles.

Happy to jump on a 30m engineering session prior to the POC to align measurement instrumentation.

—Rafael
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
rafael_mendes@redwood.com

Thanks Rafael — that's really helpful and aligns with our thinking. A few quick replies: 
- We'll prioritize SSE for the web clients and can fall back to WebSocket for mobile if needed.
- We'll aim for the 13B quantized variant as a starting point and will include average token lengths in the prompt doc by EOD.
- We're comfortable with the POC on Feb 18. Please send the test plan and POC access requirements (egress IPs, expected traffic shape).

Regarding contractual SLO: we understand warmup constraints. After the POC we'd be open to an SLO for p95 with an agreed buffer window (e.g., committed 120ms if our target is 100ms, with SLA credits defined). We can loop in procurement after we see POC numbers.

I'll add a short list of expected prompts to the Drive doc and confirm egress IPs with infra. Looking forward to the POC.

—Jordan
Senior Engineering Manager | RetailCo
